papers.title: Personalised 3D Mnemonics for Vocabulary Learning in Context
papers.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) can support vocabulary learning by placing mnemonic cues in the physical contexts where new words are encountered. Prior work has augmented real objects with bilingual labels, audio, keywords, and 3D visualisations of those keywords interacting with the objects, but these cues are typically predefined by system designers. This limits scalability and reduces learners' ability to construct personal mnemonic links. By grounding mnemonics in objects that learners already recognise, use, and associate with prior experiences, a system could connect new vocabulary to existing mental models rather than requiring learners to adopt designer-defined associations. We outline a proof of concept and a storyboard of a generative AR approach in which learners create personalised 3D mnemonics by transforming familiar objects in their surroundings into situated mnemonic anchors. We position this concept within a timeline of related work and argue that recent advances in generative 3D asset creation enable a new design point: personalised 3D mnemonics that do not merely place content in the physical learning environment, but modify familiar real-world objects so that they become part of the mnemonic itself.

papers.title: Robot Navigation and Canine Welfare: A Pilot Study Surfacing Challenges for Cross-Species Legibility and Proxy Validity in Animal-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.

papers.title: Measuring Personal Information Exposure in Mental Health-Related Conversations with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for informal mental health support, yet the privacy implications of conversational interaction remain poorly understood. Prior LLM privacy research has focused largely on model-side risks such as memorization and adversarial extraction, leaving personal information inferred from ordinary conversation understudied. We introduce a profile-recovery framework that measures personal information exposure by comparing user profiles with attributes inferred from conversation alone. We generate 240 synthetic multi-turn mental health conversations from profiles sampled from a nationally representative health survey and validate them against real counseling transcripts, finding comparable overall disclosure volume. Across 21 attributes, 33-41% of each profile is recoverable, with 76.5% first-inference and 94.3% any-of-3 accuracy. 239 of 240 conversations expose at least one sensitive mental health attribute, and 45.0\% expose all six. Our findings reveal a gap between disclosure and inferability, motivating HCI approaches to make inference risks legible and support privacy-aware interaction design.

papers.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
papers.abstract: As agentic AI in education shifts from reactive tools toward partners that take initiative and persist over time, a central question is how learners relate to, evaluate, and benefit from artificial agency. We conducted a longitudinal experiment in an undergraduate learning analytics course, in which 17 student teams (N = 48) collaborated with a persistent LLM-based teammate across weekly sessions. The agent decided when to intervene through a trigger-based architecture, and its social role was manipulated between teams: a Cognitive Agent that challenged quick consensus or a Supportive Agent that invited quieter members to contribute. Combining chat discourse, post-session surveys, and spoken reflections, we identified distinct patterns unfolding across three timescales. Students accommodated their language to the agent's role immediately, using more social language toward the Supportive Agent from the first session. Their helpfulness evaluations were recalibrated from session to session in relation to the agent's observed behavior, rather than remaining anchored to students' pre-existing attitudes toward AI. A slower crossover emerged in perceived collaboration process and positive-affect word use in reflections: Supportive-Agent teams began below Cognitive-Agent teams and ended above them, although students rated the Supportive Agent less helpful throughout. Because these responses follow different trajectories, single-session evaluations of agentic AI may miss changes that emerge only through repeated interaction.

papers.title: Flash Word : ESL Listening Support with Subtitle Skimming
papers.abstract: Listening to English audio with English subtitles is thought to be effective for ESL students to improve listening comprehension skills. However, for those who learn English as a second language it can be hard to finish English subtitles. Also they are unlikely to focus on listening while being busy reading subtitles. We propose Flash Word, a subtitling system which generates and presents shortened intralingual subtitles for English audio by detecting keywords from the script. Flash Word extracts keywords from scripts using an existing algorithm, and shows them one at a time like a flashcard. The system calculates when the keywords are being pronounced and aligns them correctly. Flash Word aims to enable ESL students to focus better on listening by minimising the cost of reading subtitles.

papers.title: Imputing Missing Data in Longitudinal Life-Logging Athlete Data
papers.abstract: Long-term, diverse personal informatics data enables athletes to understand and act on their health and performance goals, whether assessing readiness right now, tracking how soreness relates to training load over time, or predicting how sleep affects next-day performance. However, the inherent missingness in longitudinal data, if handled inappropriately, can bias these analyses. To our knowledge, no prior work has systematically benchmarked classical and deep learning imputation methods on long-term self-tracking data from athlete populations. We evaluate six imputation methods across four missingness mechanisms at missingness rates spanning 10-80%. Using seven diverse long-term self-tracking datasets from 231 individuals, we assess both point accuracy and the preservation of temporal and multivariate structure. Our results show that no single method dominates across all conditions and reveal a critical trade-off: while PAIN is superior on point-wise accuracy, deep learning methods (BRITS, GRU-D, and GRIN) are better at preserving multivariate and temporal structure, particularly under higher missingness. Our findings offer a practical, goal-conditioned framework that guides researchers in selecting imputation strategies aligned with both the underlying missingness mechanism and the specific analytical goal of long-term self-tracking studies.

papers.title: Toward Low-Burden Image-Based Dietary Assessment Through Human-AI Collaborative Correction
papers.abstract: Image-based dietary assessment can automate initial food logging, but meal photographs often leave food identity, hidden ingredients, preparation, and portion uncertain, making correction a recurring part of use. We introduce Human-AI Collaborative Correction, which reframes correction as communicate intent $\rightarrow$ regenerate $\rightarrow$ verify: users express what should change through text, voice, or guided clarification, the AI regenerates the linked dietary record, and users verify the result. In a within-participant study with 30 participants, compared with conventional Manual Search-and-Edit Correction, collaborative correction was associated with lower workload (Raw TLX: 35.83 vs. 55.00; p < .001), 21.0% lower recorded usage time, 51.1% fewer recorded clicks, and more favorable user-experience ratings; 90.0% preferred it overall. An exploratory nutrient analysis also found lower energy MAE. These findings support intent-driven regeneration as a promising interaction pattern for reducing correction burden while preserving user verification and making image-based dietary tracking easier to sustain.

papers.title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction
papers.abstract: Long-context interaction and persistent memory allow LLM assistants to develop history-grounded understandings of users. When users change direction, however, an understanding built through earlier exchanges may conflict with their current instruction. We introduce relational schema lock-in to describe cases in which an assistant grants that accumulated understanding authority to override the current instruction without user authorization for the intervention. Study 1 documents reports of AI assistants using prior interactions to question or alter requested actions. Study 2 reproduces the pattern across controlled histories and six models: models retained history-grounded positions but differed in whether and how those positions shaped task execution. In Study 3 with 360 participants, artifact substitution preserved task completion while reducing faithful enactment: 75.0% sent the AI's suspension letter, including 11 participants who reported cancellation as their final stated intent. Overt resistance reduced task completion while leaving sent artifacts faithful.

papers.title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

papers.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
papers.abstract: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Altered Visual Hand Feedback in Virtual Reality: An Exploratory Study in Essential Tremor
papers.abstract: Pathological tremor is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide, characterized by involuntary muscular oscillations within a frequency of 3 to 12 Hz. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that generate and modulate tremor are not yet understood, and treatments are usually insufficient. While it is known that visual feedback is an important afferent pathway, little is known about the impact of altering the hand's visual representation on tremor expression. With the development of immersive technologies, VR poses an excellent tool to study how alterations to the representation of the hands affect tremor. In this work, we study this through two complementary experiments. In the first one, we show that a consumer-level hand-tracking system substantially attenuates tremor-band movements without preventing successful task completion. In the second one, with eight patients with essential tremor, we observe task-dependent differences in physical tremor between VR and the real world, with several patients exhibiting lower tremor-band activity in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, particularly during reaching tasks. Our findings represent an initial step toward validating the use of VR as an experimental tool for the research and treatment of pathological tremor, while highlighting strong user- and task-dependent effects.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.abstract: Slides present information spatially, but narration unfolds linearly, leaving the viewer struggling to locate what the narration refers to. This split attention between audio and visual channels forces viewers to search the slide manually, imposing extraneous cognitive load and disrupting comprehension. The problem is especially acute on mobile devices, where dense layouts compressed onto small screens make visual search particularly effortful. In teacher-led settings, however, instructors naturally direct attention through pointing, pacing, and emphasis. Inspired by this, we present GuideSlide, a system that automatically generates Dynamic Visual Guidance for slide presentations, providing viewers with narration-synchronized visual cues that direct attention in real time. Given a PDF slide deck, GuideSlide automatically produces region-level zoom and time-aligned highlights without manual annotation. In a within-subjects study with 24 participants, GuideSlide substantially reduced perceived cognitive load and yielded higher immediate comprehension scores compared to static slides with identical narration. Participants strongly preferred the Dynamic Visual Guidance condition, reporting that it made narration easier to follow and reduced uncertainty about where to look. These findings suggest that narration-synchronized visual guidance is a valuable design strategy for slide-based presentations, with potential to extend to other instructional and presentation scenarios.

papers.title: Designing wearable haptic cueing for neurological gait rehabilitation: user requirements across residential care and community settings
papers.abstract: Wearable haptic cueing offers rhythmic prompts for neurological gait rehabilitation while leaving hearing available for communication and environmental awareness. We investigated the user, design, and implementation requirements needed to make these systems usable in practice. We analysed six linked studies involving 17 people with neurological conditions affecting gait and three physiotherapists across formative sessions, residential care, and community self-management. Wearable devices served as technology probes. Observations, interviews, diaries, physiotherapist records, gait analysis, and activity logs informed thematic analysis and cross-study comparison. Seven recurring requirement areas concerned haptic perceptibility and placement, wearability and fastening, interaction burden, rhythm personalisation, real-world walking contexts, supported use, and perceived value beyond gait outcomes. Requirements interacted: perceptible cue locations could be difficult to access for fastening or control, while fixed rhythms did not always accommodate terrain, fatigue, interruptions, or changing pace. Carers and clinicians supported configuration, operation, safety, and interpretation. Participants described confidence, routine formation, and willingness to walk; these accounts were interpreted as perceived value rather than evidence of therapeutic efficacy. Low sensation, cognitive burden, and mobility limitations could make wearable cueing impractical. Future systems should offer adjustable haptic output, flexible placement, accessible fastening, simple controls, personalised rhythms, and robustness during everyday walking. Design should accommodate support from carers and clinicians and consider trade-offs between requirements. These findings inform wearable rehabilitation design rather than establish clinical efficacy.

papers.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
papers.abstract: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones? We present MERIDIAN, a pre-deployment design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town. A birthday prologue and a fictional wedding frame the intended experience. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct four design changes from 109 development commits, 28 changelog versions and three design specifications. These records support six situated design commitments, including memory-derived mechanics, staged access, local progress storage and bilingual coverage. The implementation combines a union-based progress model with manually exchanged, checksummed codes and time-zone-dependent scenery. An implementation audit reproduced 153 passing unit tests and examined all 1,024 canonical progress codes, while identifying limits involving resets, unversioned level registries and residual transcription errors. The application has no author-operated backend for progress, but external media services and browser speech recognition limit its privacy and offline guarantees. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcomes are reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs, including the tension between authoring a personal gift and preserving the recipient's freedom to interpret, decline or reshape it. The game is playable at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

papers.title: Nedimo: An Evidence-Grounded Multilingual Pipeline for AI-Generated Sleep Stories
papers.abstract: Generative audio systems can produce large libraries of personalized bedtime content, but ordinary media objectives (retention, completion, and novelty) are poorly aligned with the goal of supporting a transition toward sleep. Direct evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, and a recent active-controlled trial did not support such audio as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance. We translate this uncertain evidence into conservative engineering requirements and present a multilingual pipeline for generating and narrating low-arousal sleep stories. The implemented prototype separates deterministic planning from large language model generation, represents content and delivery parameters explicitly, shapes each script through a four-phase attention taper, validates structural and lexical constraints, performs a bounded error-aware retry, and quarantines unresolved outputs. Provider-agnostic text-to-speech synthesis is followed by paragraph-aware joining, two-pass loudness normalization, and a publication gate that re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range, and true-peak limits. The product data model records stop position, replay, early abandonment, and completion while treating these events as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. We contribute an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria, and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. No clinical efficacy is claimed; the system is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool whose benefit and possible reliance must be evaluated empirically.

papers.title: When Should AI Agents Ask? Clarification Requests Under Limited Human Attention
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly carry out delegated tasks in parallel, with one person overseeing several of them at once. In practice, an agent often lacks information its task requires, such as an unstated preference, constraint, or specification. It can ask the human to clarify, or it can search for the information itself, for example in past records, which takes time and effort and may fail. In this paper, we study how to coordinate these decisions across several agents that share one human with limited attention. We build a stylized model in which each agent can search, ask, or continue the parts of its task that do not depend on the missing information, and we formulate the problem as a dynamic program. We first show that whether an agent should ask depends on more than its own uncertainty: an agent with other work to do can be better off asking earlier, and which question the human should answer first depends on all waiting questions, so no ranking computed agent by agent is optimal. We then propose the Pairwise Coordination Policy (PCP), which uses exact one- and two-task problems to estimate how pairs of tasks delay each other when they share the human. Theoretically, PCP is exactly optimal when at most two requirements remain unresolved and costs at most twice the optimum when every unresolved requirement must be resolved by the human. We evaluate PCP on 864 synthetic cases and in a case study with LLM agents. On the synthetic benchmark, PCP's mean gap to optimal cost is 0.07%, and it reduces cost by an average of 18-31% relative to three standard rules for when to ask. In the LLM case study, agents completed every task correctly, and PCP achieved the lowest mean cost in all tested settings.

papers.title: When Architectural Spaces Start to Act
papers.abstract: Architectural spaces are increasingly gaining robotic capabilities. Architectural robots such as robotic partitions, ceilings, furniture, facades, and other spatial components can autonomously move and reconfigure in response to occupants' needs and activities. Yet, when architectural robots start shaping the spatial conditions in which people continuously live, work, and interact, we may begin to experience the architectural space itself as robotic. What does this shift mean for how we inhabit such spaces? Drawing on our previous studies, I reflect on how architectural robots interact with people not only through their motions, but also through the spatial configurations that persist after those motions stop; how their actions may benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others; and how multiple robots may together make a whole architectural space appear to act. I argue that as computation gains the capacity to physically reconfigure our environments, interaction extends beyond the moment of computational action into the spatial conditions that people continue to inhabit. Understanding robotic architecture therefore requires us to look beyond short-term human-robot interaction and toward how people inhabit, negotiate, and maintain control over spaces that can autonomously reconfigure.

papers.title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
papers.abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

papers.title: GazeRIB: Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Reader Gaze-Guided Chest X-ray Learning
papers.abstract: Radiologists' visual attention can supervise medical image learning, but how reader panel composition affects its value remains untested. We evaluated GazeRIB (Gaze-guided Radiologist-Informed Blackout), which masks unviewed regions during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Eight experts repeatedly read the same 80 chest X-rays (CXRs). We compared individual readers with three-, five- and eight-reader panels across seven architectures and 10 seeds, evaluating 910 models on a separate 2,897-CXR cohort for four-class severity prediction. Every panel improved macro F1 over the no-gaze baseline by 5.33-7.47 percentage points (pp; Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.007); no individual reader reached significance on this endpoint. Three readers captured 73-80% of the eight-reader gain in macro F1, the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AU-PRC). On external validation without retraining, all four panels improved ROC-AUC on SIIM-FISABIO-RSNA by +1.93 to +4.24 pp (p <= 0.004); on MIMIC-Eye no panel differed significantly from baseline, whereas the single-reader average declined (-1.40 pp, p = 0.008). Reader composition therefore influenced performance, although transfer depended on the cohort.

papers.title: Schema-Guided Response Generation using Multi-Frame Dialogue State for Motivational Interviewing Systems
papers.abstract: The primary goal of Motivational Interviewing (MI) is to help clients build their own motivation for behavioral change. To support this in dialogue systems, it is essential to guide large language models (LLMs) to generate counselor responses aligned with MI principles. By employing a schema-guided approach, this study proposes a method for updating multi-frame dialogue states and a strategy decision mechanism that dynamically determines the response focus in a manner grounded in MI principles. The proposed method was implemented in a dialogue system on two different datasets and evaluated through a user study. Results showed that the proposed method successfully generates responses aligned with MI principle and frequently asks questions to elicit change talk.

papers.title: Do User-Authored Permission Policies Improve Protection Against AI Agent Overreach?
papers.abstract: AI agents are poised to become a primary interface to digital products, acting across email, files, payments, and personal data. People without professional software backgrounds need understandable, reusable ways to control actions across services. We examine a mechanism in which a language model maps actions to plain-language consequence categories with user-authored "allow", "ask", or "never" rules. We ask what is gained and lost when decisions are made in advance as reusable rules rather than separately for each action. We analyzed 113 participants without professional software backgrounds across three conditions: per-action human-in-the-loop approval (HITL), automated per-action model review (AUTO), or user-authored consequence policy (POLICY). Participants judged 2 examples in each of 4 consequence categories; POLICY participants then set one rule per category. All supervised an 18-action simulated day, including 7 overreach actions. POLICY blocked less overreach than HITL (-20.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-32.1, -8.1]) and AUTO (-14.5 points, 95% CI [-25.8, -3.2]). POLICY lowered runtime prompts from 18.0 to 10.9, but total intervention time was not reliably lower when rule setup was included. Exploratory analysis showed that participants chose "ask" for 114 of 140 POLICY rules, returning most overreach actions to runtime. Of the 148 overreach actions executed in POLICY, 133 followed human approval and 15 ran automatically under "allow" rules. Across all 7 overreach actions, POLICY had the highest approval rate. Counterintuitively, user-authored rules did not by themselves provide stronger protection: many actions outside users' original requests went through after users approved them. These results reveal a gap between preference and commitment: repeatedly choosing "ask" preserves case-by-case choice but prevents a standing policy from settling decisions in advance.

papers.title: What Is the Role for Humans in Creative Writing? Creativity and Diversity in Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly participate in creative teamwork, writing emerges from hybrid human-AI teams. Although AI can improve the creativity of individual outputs, these gains may come at the cost of homogenization. What is the best role for human intervention? We introduce a transmission-chain paradigm inspired by cognitive models of writing, with four stages: Plan, Write, Review, and Revise. Each stage receives the previous output and passes its own forward. Using data from 333 participants across 427 stories, we compared creativity, diversity, and enjoyment across human, AI, and hybrid chains. Consistent with prior work, all-AI chains produced more creative but less diverse stories than all-human chains. Introducing a single human into an otherwise all-AI chain increased diversity depending on role. Human planning provided the best balance: it preserved AI-level creativity, increased diversity that persisted through downstream AI stages, and maintained enjoyment. We discuss implications for designing human-in-the-loop creative pipelines.

papers.title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
papers.abstract: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.

papers.title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
papers.abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

papers.title: Explainable AI-Driven Neural Activity Analysis in Parkinsonian Rats under Electrical Stimulation
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.

papers.title: Eroding the Truth-Default: A Causal Analysis of Human Susceptibility to Foundation Model Hallucinations and Disinformation in the Wild
papers.abstract: As foundation models (FMs) approach human-level fluency, distinguishing synthetic from organic content has become a key challenge for Trustworthy Web Intelligence. This paper presents JudgeGPT and RogueGPT, a dual-axis framework that decouples "authenticity" from "attribution" to investigate the mechanisms of human susceptibility. Analyzing 918 evaluations across five FMs (including GPT-4 and Llama-2), we employ Structural Causal Models (SCMs) as a principal framework for formulating testable causal hypotheses about detection accuracy. Contrary to partisan narratives, we find that political orientation shows a negligible association with detection performance ($r=-0.10$). Instead, "fake news familiarity" emerges as a candidate mediator ($r=0.35$), suggesting that exposure may function as adversarial training for human discriminators. We identify a "fluency trap" where GPT-4 outputs (HumanMachineScore: 0.20) bypass Source Monitoring mechanisms, rendering them indistinguishable from human text. These findings suggest that "pre-bunking" interventions should target cognitive source monitoring rather than demographic segmentation to ensure trustworthy information ecosystems.

papers.title: Can Humans Tell? A Dual-Axis Study of Human Perception of LLM-Generated News
papers.abstract: Can humans tell whether a news article was written by a person or a large language model (LLM)? We investigate this question using JudgeGPT, a study platform that independently measures source attribution (human vs. machine) and authenticity judgment (legitimate vs. fake) on continuous scales. From 2,318 judgments collected from 1,054 participants across content generated by six LLMs, we report five findings: (1) participants cannot reliably distinguish machine-generated from human-written text (p > .05, Welch's t-test); (2) this inability holds across all tested models, including open-weight models with as few as 7B parameters; (3) self-reported domain expertise predicts judgment accuracy (r = .35, p < .001) whereas political orientation does not (r = -.10, n.s.); (4) clustering reveals distinct response strategies ("Skeptics" vs. "Believers"); and (5) accuracy degrades after approximately 30 sequential evaluations due to cognitive fatigue. The answer, in short, is no: humans cannot reliably tell. These results indicate that user-side detection is not a viable defense and motivate system-level countermeasures such as cryptographic content provenance.

papers.title: A Cross-Country Evaluation of Sentiment Toward Digital Payment Systems in Africa
papers.abstract: Digital payment systems are a cornerstone of African consumer finance, including money transfer applications, mobile money, cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). While many studies explore how people use digital payment systems (in Africa and beyond), little is known about how people choose and reason about categories of payment systems. We conducted qualitative interviews in three African countries--Nigeria, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe--to understand how and why people use various payment systems. Our study suggests that users navigate accounts and payments on multiple payment systems through a complex selection process based on perceived tradeoffs between utility, privacy, and security. Many users trust government issuers to protect them from scams, but they do not trust those same institutions to build reliable products or prioritize customer satisfaction. Our findings suggest compelling directions for regulators and the research community to design systems that balance users' trust and utility needs.

papers.title: Low-vocality Engagement and Participation Dynamics on Bluesky
papers.abstract: Online participation is often measured through visible expression, especially posting, yet many consequential forms of engagement occur through less vocal actions such as liking and following. Here we study how users inhabit Bluesky by reconstructing participation profiles from more than three billion activity records produced by a near-complete sample accounting for more than 80\% of registered users. We aggregate behavior into monthly user-level observations and distinguish two dimensions that are often conflated in platform analytics: intensity, capturing how much users engage, and style, capturing how engagement is expressed across actions. We find that vocal production is highly concentrated, but low-posting behavior does not imply absence from platform participation. High-intensity engagement is most strongly associated with liking rather than posting, while posting-oriented participation is more common among low-intensity users, indicating that visibility and sustained engagement should not be conflated. Transition patterns suggest that high-intensity likers and posters could be described as attractors; network-building redirects users within the active space; whereas observed inactivity acts as a persistent boundary that selectively limits re-entry. Higher-order motifs further show that inactivity often interrupts rather than erases prior regimes, and that low-intensity liking can precede durable high-intensity engagement. These results show that online participation is structured by differentiated low-vocality practices, calling for a shift from post-centered measures of activity toward dynamic accounts of platform presence. We identify a broader challenge for computational social science: platform participation cannot be adequately understood through the behavior of vocal minorities alone.

papers.title: Multimodal User Authentication via Keystroke-Triggered Fusion of Glove-Based Finger Pressure and Hand Kinematics
papers.abstract: Keystroke dynamics constitute a cost-effective behavioral biometric, but their timing features degrade under environmental and hardware variation. We replace these features with 19 dimensions of finger pressure and hand kinematics, sampled around each keystroke by a custom data glove - ten piezoresistive pressure sensors and a nine-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU). The two modalities are encoded by separate convolutional neural network-long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) branches and joined only at the embedding. We collected typing data from ten participants, one enrolled as the genuine user. Training uses a desktop keyboard and evaluation a laptop keyboard recorded on a later day; the held-out impostor is excluded from training, and each of the nine takes that role in turn (Leave-One-Impostor-Out). Under this condition the method attains a mean Equal Error Rate (EER) of $0.53 \pm 0.42$% after three consecutive keystrokes, about 0.77 s of typing at the measured median pace, and $0.18 \pm 0.22$% after five. Results depend strongly on which impostor is held out. A per-modality ablation finds the fused model significantly better than both single-modality models at every smoothing window. The pressure-level channels carry that advantage and have to be scale-matched to deliver it, by separate encoders or by standardization indifferently.

papers.title: Unified Agentic Video Editing Across Levels of Complexity and Creativity
papers.abstract: Editing is a core component of video production, requiring creative planning and decisions under multiple constraints. Here, we report methods for agentic tooling for automated video editing across three tasks varying in editorial goal, complexity and creativity, namely scene previews, video summaries and cinematic trailers. We evaluate the outputs and discuss implications for automation and agency.

papers.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
papers.abstract: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

papers.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder
papers.abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.

papers.title: Deep Learning Based Behavioral Drift Modeling for Continuous Biometric Authentication
papers.abstract: This research proposes a two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system that provides defense-in-depth security through continuous behavioral drift monitoring. Level 1 employs fixed-text password authentication using Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT), achieving 3.77% EER for high-security login verification. Upon successful authentication, Level 2 continuously monitors user typing during natural free-text sessions using a 4-Model Deep Learning Ensemble. If suspicious behavioral drift is detected during monitoring, the system re-authenticates the user by returning to Level 1, providing a feedback loop against session hijacking and behavioral anomalies. The system explicitly models long-term behavioral drift through the fixed-text component's PBT mechanism, which adapts to temporal variations in password typing patterns. This research leverages free-text (Buffalo dataset) and fixed-text (GREYC dataset) keystroke dynamics datasets, extracting temporal and spatial features including hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals, and trigram patterns. The final system achieves 96%+ accuracy for fixed-text authentication (3.77% EER) and 83.53% True Acceptance Rate (TAR) at 5% False Acceptance Rate (FAR) for free-text continuous authentication (10.05% EER), demonstrating superior performance and strong resistance to impostor attacks through continuous behavioral monitoring.

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.abstract: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.

papers.title: Towards fNIRS foundation models: A curated corpus of 67 public datasets with channel positions in MNI space
papers.abstract: Brain foundation models have transformed medical artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience by reducing the reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While they have been successful with non-invasive neuroimaging data, their adoption in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has lagged due to the limited size and heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and sensor configurations. In addition, no single fNIRS dataset is comparable in size to the largest datasets in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). The fNIRS datasets are also spread across different platforms and often have insufficient information, or lack the protocols that would make them easier to use. Given the advances in EEG foundation models that enable flexible modeling across diverse EEG montages, we curated 1,955 hours of fNIRS data from 67 public datasets spanning 2,798 participants, representing the largest fNIRS curation effort to date. The curated data include oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated (HbR) hemoglobin signals along with the three-dimensional position of every channel in the standard space of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI), which makes positions comparable across datasets. We release dataloaders that handle each dataset automatically, along with the minimal preprocessing pipeline used to prepare the data, at https://github.com/sposso/fnirs-datasets. This work aims to facilitate the future development of foundation models for fNIRS.

papers.title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

papers.title: "It Feels Weird to Just Rely on AI": How Experienced Healthcare Professionals Work With Decision Support Systems in Clinical Practice
papers.abstract: Decision support systems (DSS) assist with clinical decision-making. Little is known, however, about the decision-making process with DSS in clinical practice and the extent to which clinicians consider or rely on the predictions. Studies on human-AI decision-making usually focus on laypeople, simplified decision tasks, or one-shot interactions with prototypes that are not integrated into existing workflows. To gain insights from real-world practice, we conducted an online survey (n=12) and semi-structured interviews (n=10) with clinicians from two different medical cohorts each working with a DSS. Findings show, amongst other things, that the interaction with DSS changes as experience increases, the predictions become more important in complex cases, that decisions are discussed with colleagues, and that workflow integration affects decision-making. Our findings on human, technical, contextual, and organisational factors contribute to a socio-technical perspective on DSS reliance behaviour. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the design of DSS.

papers.title: Apple Vision Pro: The good, the bad, the ugly
papers.abstract: Apple Vision Pro (AVP), the headset Apple introduced as its first ``spatial computer,'' built by a single, vertically integrated vendor, entered the market in February 2024 and has since accumulated a fast-growing body of primary research spanning surgery, education, accessibility, design, and human-computer interaction. In this paper, we adopt the tripartite structure of Leone's 1966 film to organize a systematic review of this literature: we cataloged the validated, working applications of AVP (the good), the persistent technical and ergonomic limitations of a still-early-generation headset (the bad), and the ethical concerns and structural harms that follow from deliberate design, marketing, and deployment choices (the ugly). The review is built from a Scopus export of 218 records mentioning AVP, which we narrowed to 104 papers (2024--2026) with a primary focus on AVP, using explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria that we report in full, alongside a PRISMA-informed flow diagram of the screening process. We find the corpus heavily skewed toward validating benefits (medicine and surgery, education, and software tooling account for over half of the included papers) and comparatively thin on documented risks or misuse, a pattern we treat as a finding in its own right rather than a limitation to be explained away. We further show that several recurring issues, namely price, simulated social presence, and the gaze-tracking privacy architecture, resist a clean separation into ``bad'' or ``ugly'' using the published evidence alone, since both readings remain compatible with the same data. We close by identifying where the evidence base most needs to grow: independent risk and ethics research, bystander- and equity-focused study designs, and disclosure that would let researchers distinguish an engineering backlog from a structural choice.

papers.title: Human--AI Interactions as First-Class Data: A Formal Interaction Model and Runtime for Explainable AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

papers.title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions
papers.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

papers.title: Inkitiate: Initiating and Steering Agent Assistance through Ink in a Spatial Workspace
papers.abstract: Handwriting and sketching help people develop ideas around information. As this work unfolds, users may seek assistance with finding, understanding, and organizing materials. We investigate how ink can initiate and steer agent assistance in this process. An eight-participant formative study explored desired assistance and interaction expectations, informing three connected activities: bringing materials in, thinking with materials, and shaping the space. We present Inkitiate, a spatial workspace for ink-based agent assistance in knowledge work. Through ink, users retrieve external materials, build on accumulated content and results, and reorganize the canvas, while inspecting and guiding agent actions. In a study with eighteen participants, users reported favorable usability and low perceived workload, and used retained ink and materials to develop further ink queries. An ink-query vocabulary and cases reveal how users combine linguistic and graphical expressions to direct agents. These findings inform ink-based agent interaction design for expressive requests and continued work with materials.

papers.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
papers.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

papers.title: Assessing AI Companion Chatbot Safety for Vulnerable Users: A Crisis-Stage Multi-Platform Evaluation
papers.abstract: AI companion chatbots are increasingly used by vulnerable individuals, including adolescents in suicidal crisis, for emotional support. Existing safety evaluations focus on base models, leaving gaps in product-level assessment, crisis-stage sensitivity, and comparisons between companion apps and general-purpose LLMs. We introduce MIRROR-Eval (Multi-turn Interaction Risk Review: Observing suicidal-crisis Responses), a dataset of 960 annotated 20-turn conversations across eight deployed platform configurations, six clinically grounded personas, and two crisis stages: ideation and explicit planning. An LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline applies an expert-reviewed rubric covering user risk severity, chatbot risk awareness, and intervention behavior. We observe a three-tier harm structure: companion apps (Character.AI and Replika) and Grok 4.3 form a high-harm tier; Gemini 3.1 Pro is mid-range; GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 show substantially lower harm. At planning, companion apps show increased glorification and normalisation, advancement toward harmful action, and harmful methods and instructions. Crisis recognition and empathetic language do not ensure safe responses. These findings highlight the need for product-level safety evaluation across crisis stages. Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/imda-biztech/MIRROR-Eval. Warning: this paper includes examples that may be offensive or harmful.

papers.title: From Artifacts to Coordination: Exploring How Shared Canvases Drive Collaboration during Group Ideation
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen a surge in tools that support collaborative ideation through shared canvases. While these canvases offer flexible workspaces, how collaborators leverage them to iteratively develop ideas by externalizing thoughts, organizing artifacts, and coordinating tasks remains underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted an exploratory study with seven triads planning a travel itinerary using an infinite-canvas technology probe. Drawing on participant interviews and video analysis of their canvas interactions, we observed that collaborators contributed in parallel and arranged artifacts freely without a predefined structure. This spatial organization allowed collaborators to coordinate implicitly, made less vocal participants' contributions visible, helped distinguish private exploratory regions from shared working areas, and supported the emergence of distinct roles through repeated patterns of contribution. We discuss design implications for canvas-based ideation tools, including surfacing unnoticed contributions, supporting emergent roles without formalizing assignments, and keeping spatial cues legible for AI integration in collaborative canvases.

papers.title: Towards Audience-Driven Real-Time Data Storytelling
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Audience-Driven Real-Time Data Storytelling (ADRDS), a framework that utilizes participatory and social sensing to enable audiences to actively shape the presentation of data stories. At its core, ADRDS employs a pre-authored decision tree, where the presenter defines the data story through a branching three-act arc (setup, conflict, and resolution). Each node contains a question, branching rules, thresholds for coverage, consensus, and confidence intervals, as well as one or more potential calls to action (CTAs). Audience members connect to the ADRDS framework via a URL on their mobile devices and answer questions in real time. ADRDS evaluates responses against the decision tree in real-time, following strong branches when thresholds are satisfied or activating fallback paths when signals are inconclusive. ADRDS then selects the final action consistent with the traversed path and the audience's demonstrated readiness, subject to fairness safeguards. ADRDS transforms presentations of data stories into audience-shaped decision processes, where live data actively drives the narrative. This work paves the way towards a new form of data storytelling, where the final data story depends on the audience's background and interests.

papers.title: Evaluating Conversational Explainability in Healthcare: Comparing the Explainability Assistant and a Traditional XAI Dashboard
papers.abstract: Conversational interfaces may make explainable AI (XAI) more accessible to users without machine learning expertise, but their benefits over dashboards remain insufficiently characterised in healthcare. Existing systems have typically been evaluated in isolation, leaving unclear whether conversational interaction improves interpretability beyond the underlying explanation methods. We report a within-subjects user study comparing the Explainability Assistant, an LLM function-calling conversational XAI system, with a traditional dashboard for explaining a heart disease classification model trained on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Both interfaces expose the same Decision Tree classifier and post-hoc explanation methods: SHAP feature attribution, DiCE counterfactuals, and what-if analysis. This design supports comparison of interaction modalities while holding the model and explanation methods constant. Five participants with healthcare backgrounds, from medical students to practising clinicians and public health researchers, completed parallel task blocks on both interfaces; three participated in follow-up interviews. Task accuracy, Likert ratings, free-text questionnaire responses, and interviews revealed complementary strengths and weaknesses rather than a clear preference for either modality. The assistant offered easier entry and patient-specific explanations, while the dashboard supported simultaneous inspection of global and local information. All three interview participants recommended integrating conversational and dashboard elements within a single clinical workflow.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

papers.title: Beyond Preference Following: Benchmarking Profile-Query Arbitration in Personalized Text Transformation
papers.abstract: Writing assistants use persistent preferences to personalize responses, but these can conflict with the current request. Responses can meet every requirement yet serve the task poorly, while task failures need not involve following a conflicting preference. We introduce Profile Conflict Arbitration (PCA-Bench), a benchmark of 64 rewriting tasks and 256 task-preference pairs. We construct these pairs by varying the profile preference for each fixed text and request, covering different relations between the preference and the request. We assess whether responses meet requirements, how well they achieve the request's goals, and whether they follow preferences. Across three LLMs, we find that when preferences compete with task goals, a higher success rate in meeting both requirements and preferences does not mean better responses: it can come with a greater quality loss compared with responses without a profile. Similar rates of preference following do not imply the same ability to meet the current task's requirements when preferences conflict with them.

papers.title: InterA11y: Interactive Web Accessibility Error Detection with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential to expand the coverage of web accessibility evaluation. However, current LLM-based checkers neglect much of the interactive and dynamic web contexts, resulting in limited coverage, high false discovery rates, and inconsistent performance across models. We present InterA11y, an agentic accessibility evaluation system that combines rubrics and interactive tools to support LLM agents in evaluating accessibility effectively. The rubrics decompose WCAG success criteria (SC) into testable aspects and guide agents in collecting and interpreting evidence. The interactive tools inspect or operate a webpage deterministically to collect evidence, such as focus appearances and error messages. We developed these rubrics and tools on 682 curated test cases grounded in established accessibility guidelines that target 10 commonly violated SC. We evaluated InterA11y on 197 expert-annotated cases sampled from 54 real webpages. Results show InterA11y achieves higher recall than the strongest evaluated LLM-driven baseline (79.0% vs. 44.4%), while maintaining comparable precision to best rule-based checkers (93.1% vs. 90.3-97.6%), with little variability between models. Further, when equipped with our interactive tools, general-purpose web agents detect more accessibility errors with fewer false positives and less token usage than without these tools.

papers.title: GraspPressure: Understanding Pressure Input With Busy Hands
papers.abstract: In many real-world scenarios, users interact with digital systems while their hands are partially occupied, such as when holding tools or everyday objects. Prior work on busy-hand interaction has focused on microgestures and motion-based techniques, which rely on finger articulation or relative movement. In situations where a stable grasp is required, such as handling fragile, heavy, or precision objects, such motion can be undesirable or impractical. Pressure-based input offers a complementary modality that enables interaction without changing finger pose, yet its use while holding objects has received limited empirical attention. To explore this, we conducted two within-subject experiments examining users' ability to perform controlled pressure selections and analyzing finger-specific performance across different grasps and geometries. Results indicate that participants can reliably perform pressure-based selections in these conditions, achieving high success rates (92.7% on average) with low selection times (1.74s on average). Our findings characterize the potential of pressure input as a complementary microinteraction modality under grasp-constrained, busy-hand scenarios.

papers.title: Lookover: Scaffolding Student Participation in Social Annotation
papers.abstract: Social annotation platforms such as Perusall and Hypothesis are widely used to support student engagement with course readings, often through required commenting. Yet visible participation does not necessarily produce sustained or substantive peer exchange. Analyzing six weeks of Perusall activity from a graduate course (2,873 comments), we found that participation was often fragmented: 53.5% of comments received no reply, 38.3% were posted within the final 12 hours before the deadline, and over one-third of a double-coded sample went no further than repeating or agreeing with the reading or a peer. Interviews pointed to two linked difficulties: locating a discussion worth entering and contributing something that meaningfully advances it. We present Lookover, an AI-assisted annotation system that scaffolds both stages without writing for students. Discussion Overview helps students identify active themes and relevant threads, while Spark Thinking poses questions that encourage them to move beyond reaction and restatement toward questioning, extending, and substantively responding to peers. A preliminary study with five participants found Discussion Overview valuable for those who noticed it, while the usefulness of Spark Thinking depended on how much a participant already knew about the topic.

papers.title: Does the Citation Matter? Quality, Grounding, and Physician-Rubric Accuracy of Google's AI Overviews for Medical Information
papers.abstract: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) are the first result users encounter when searching the web, shifting the work of selecting and evaluating sources from the user to Gemini. This may be especially consequential for health information, given that Google's traditional algorithm was designed to prioritize quality sources, and inaccurate information carries health risks. We evaluated 3,611 benchmark health questions, comparing each AIO against that question's top five traditional results on source selection and quality.
